We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine model-dimension cells (p < .0001); a text-invariant negative control returns chance (p = 1). On human transitions at least 0.5 points against the position trend, models recover 69-76% of valence directions and 53-68% for arousal and dominance. Under crossed participant-text resampling, all nine identity intervals remain above zero; joint-control advantages are robust for valence and directional but less certain for arousal. High shape agreement still coexists with scale bias. LitArc-Bench identifies which components of literary reader response are recoverable beyond shallow explanations and why shape, calibration, and human variability require separate evaluation.
items.author: Mingming Su, Yushan Wei, Sen Song, Xinche Zhang

items.title: Evaluating Human Sensitivity to Gender Biased AI-Generated Content through Human Assessment of Google's Autocomplete Function
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18371v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly present, but their effects on human users remain underexplored. We tested whether AI-attributed information influences views regarding gender-related statements, a domain where biases are pervasive. Spanish-speaking participants recruited through Prolific evaluated biased statements derived from Google's autocomplete function and human-authored, non-biased gender-related facts. Participants were either informed that some of the material was AI-generated or received no information about its origin. AI attribution did not affect reaction times or agreement judgments. This result suggests that AI-generated content does not automatically raise credibility concerns and may be evaluated with less scrutiny compared to human-produced content.
items.author: Tamara Serrano, Nikoleta Pantelidou, Raquel Montero, Natalia Moskvina, Paolo Morosi, Evelina Leivada

items.title: Learning Word-Level Explanations of Text Reuse in Latin Literature with Little Annotation
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detecting an intertextual reference is only the first step; philologists also need to know how a later author reworked the source. We explain a reuse pair word by word: each word of the reusing passage is first aligned to its source word, then labeled with the operation that transformed it, such as a copy, a change of inflection, or a substitution. Such word-level operations are expensive to annotate, and only a few corpora annotated at this level exist for text reuse in Latin literature. We describe a procedure that needs only a limited number of annotations: synthetic pairs, built by applying known operations to Latin text, train a first model, and active learning chooses the pairs an annotator corrects. Among several architectures, a model that links and labels together performs best: a pointer network that, for every reuse word, chooses a source word and names the operation in the same step. We show that with active learning, 200 pairs chosen by uncertainty are enough for the model to match one trained on every annotated pair of the 1,490 references of the Loci Similes benchmark. We release our code, word-level predictions for all references, and an interactive demo.
items.author: Julian Schelb, Michael Wittweiler, Marie Revellio

items.title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models *Author(s)
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18279v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.
items.author: Jiayu Feng

items.title: MamaReason: Unfinished Reasoning and Answer Recovery in Clinical Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18264v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Answer continuation often returns a diagnosis already stated in unfinished clinical reasoning. We study this behavior in MamaReason, adapted from dense Gemma 4 31B, on MamaBench's 217 paired maternal and child-health presentations. An explicit-commitment extractor identifies a diagnosis in 75 of 94 failed RL first passes and 75 of 93 failed SFT first passes. The continuation matches that diagnosis in 67/75 RL cases and 58/75 SFT cases, using diagnosis strings alone. Reading these commitments without additional generation recovers 30 of the 40 RL pairs restored by continuation under the archived correctness labels. Recurrence controls distinguish routine mentions from repeated answer selection. An offline second-commitment trigger measures the tradeoff between earlier readout and paired accuracy. The resulting decomposition separates diagnostic content already present in a trace, completion of an accepted answer, and paired diagnostic correctness. For clinical language-model evaluation, these are distinct outcomes that become visible when the same reasoning trace is examined through multiple readouts.
items.author: Thanni Adewuyi, Adepoju Jeremiah Moyondafoluwa, Dorcas Amapu, Dieko Whenu, Sylvia Essessien, Sandra Oko-Oba, Pelumi Onafadeji, Lily Aimas-Love, Samuel Omolaiye, Abiodun Adereni

items.title: NER-D: A cross-domain benchmark for German NER
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present NER-D, a cross-domain benchmark for German NER comprising 13 datasets spanning 9 domains, including General/Politics, Wikipedia, Legal, Medical, Historical, Financial, Agriculture and Archaeology. We examine the performance of both proprietary LLMs and state-of-the-art small open-source models using normal prompting and further examine the performance gains achievable via in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning. Our results show that without any sort of optimization a proprietary model (GPT-5.4 mini) outperforms the smaller open-source models on 6 out of 13 datasets, but LoRA fine-tuning enables the smaller models to substantially outperform the proprietary baseline. We further analyze the influence of the domain and the tagset used in each task on the performance achieved in the different evaluation settings. Our benchmark will be available as a resource for the development of future German NER methods on both general and specialized domains.\footnote{We make our code, data, and models publicly available upon acceptance of this paper.
items.author: Marc Brinner, Philipp Cimiano, Karolina Hanna Czok, Regina Stodden, Viju Sudhi, Sina Zarrie{\ss}

items.title: A Multi-Layered AI Pipeline for BPMN Generation from Natural Language
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The automated transformation of unstructured natural language process descriptions into Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams remains a challenging task, due to linguistic ambiguity and the difficulty to detect non-adjacent control-flow relationships. This paper proposes a solution for generating BPMN models from natural language descriptions through a multi-layered pipeline that integrates transformer-based architectures, Large Language Models and ontology population. The proposed method starts with natural language descriptions and separates textual processing, control-flow relation extraction, and structural validation into dedicated components. Entity extraction is performed using a fine-tuned RoBERTa-based transformer model while a control-flow engine captures non-adjacent relationships through LLM-based inference. To improve generalization under limited available data, the approach uses a dynamic few-shot strategy with con- trolled template input construction, enabling improved generalization under limited data availability. Additionally, an ontology population mechanism is introduced to represent the generated process models as semantic knowledge structures. For evaluation purposes we have used from the literature and industry reference processes. Additionally, we have validated the proposed method on a real-world heart disease patients transitional care process, capturing practical constraints and multi-actor collaboration, and serving as an expert-defined benchmark scenario. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance in the relation extraction task, achieving an accuracy of 90.7%, as well as maintaining structural alignment between the generated and reference BPMN models across multiple evaluation scenarios scenarios.
items.author: Alexandru Rancea, Ionut Anghel, Tudor Cioara, Ovidiu Anchidin, Ancuta Nemes

items.title: Folding Language Models into Themselves
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation usually trains a compact student from scratch, which needs a large amount of data even though the teacher's weights already encode most of what the student has to learn. In this work, we explore building the student directly from the teacher's weights. We propose Concertina, which folds every group of N adjacent teacher layers into one shared block that is executed N times. Each loop step carries a low-rank correction initialized from the layer it replaces, and a per-token gate mixes these corrections, to let every token recover the behavior of the original layers from a single shared block. We further design a distillation data recipe that balances general, mathematical, academic and targeted multiple-choice data, to recover all capabilities of the teacher together rather than one at the expense of another. On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model distilled on 22B tokens retains about 90% of the teacher on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks. It outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines, as well as Qwen3-1.7B, which is trained on over a thousand times more data. These results suggest that a compact model need not be retrained at scale, since folding the teacher into itself and distilling it on the right data recovers most of its capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/myboker/concertina.
items.author: Ziyang Zhang, Yubin Jing, Yuyao Li, Haofan Wang, Yichen Gong

items.title: Contagious Fingerprints: When LLMs Inherit Another Model's Identity
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The fingerprint by which a classifier recognizes the LLM behind a text is usually treated as a fixed property of the model. We show that it is contagious: a model that continues a conversation begun by another model inherits that model's fingerprint. This undermines audits of API relays, which can serve the first turns of a conversation with the model a customer pays for and silently hand the rest to a cheaper one. After such a handoff, detection of the substitute by a text classifier drops from 0.97 to 0.72 (DeepSeek replacing Claude Sonnet) and from 0.87 to 0.54 for a same-vendor downgrade (Haiku), and retraining on handoff data repairs only substitutes seen in training. Preregistered experiments trace the contagion to imitation of the history's style. History also moves a model away from its own fingerprint: active probes are not camouflaged, but when calibrated on fresh conversations they flag \emph{honest} models on long contexts at rates up to 1.00, and a standard MMD equality test rejects all nine models we test. Both failures come from comparing a history-dependent reply with a history-free reference. We propose \textsc{Lineup}, which samples references from the claimed model \emph{on the same history} and tests the audited reply by its rank among them. \textsc{Lineup} controls false positives by exchangeability and needs no fitted threshold or log-probabilities. With contemporaneous references on two closed models, its false-positive rate is 0.056 (preregistered bound 0.10), and it detects 0.81 of substitute sessions across six pairs after four audited turns.
items.author: Zailong Tian

items.title: VEPO: Mitigating Multilingual Hallucinations in LVLMs via Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18096v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) achieve strong multimodal performance, yet they remain prone to object hallucination---generating answers that are linguistically fluent but visually ungrounded. This issue is especially severe in low-resource languages, where weaker cross-modal alignment causes models to rely more on language priors than on image evidence. Existing remedies either require costly multilingual annotations or external translation/reward models, or intervene at inference time in ways that can distort the output language. We propose VEPO(Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization), a training-time method that transfers reliable visual grounding from English to other languages without external models. VEPO first localizes key visual evidence using English queries via mid-layer cross-modal attention, then constructs preference pairs that share the same correct answer but differ in evidence sufficiency (full image vs.\ key-region masked image). Direct preference optimization on these pairs encourages low-resource inputs to prefer answers supported by complete visual evidence. Experiments on multilingual POPE and MME with Chinese, French, and Hindi show consistent hallucination reduction and perception gains, with the largest improvements on the lowest-resource language. Analyses further confirm that VEPO sharpens question-relevant attention and that evidence-guided masking outperforms random masking.
items.author: Chengpeng Fu, Xiaocheng Feng, Wenshuai Huo, Yichong Huang, Baohang Li, Duyu Tang, Ting Liu

items.title: Agent-as-a-Judge
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18067v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence has progressed from task-specific systems toward general models spanning perception, generation, reasoning, and autonomous interaction, making reliable evaluation essential for comparison, deployment, and post-training feedback. At scale, modern evaluation pipelines increasingly rely on LLM-as-a-Judge to produce scores, preferences, and critiques; in its fixed-context setting, the judge relies on the supplied evaluand and evaluation materials. Yet a reliable verdict may require evidence beyond the supplied evaluand and context---either because critical environmental states remain unrecorded in the static execution log, or because controversial factual claims require external verification. Passive judges cannot obtain that missing evidence before deciding, especially when evaluating agent trajectories, executable artifacts, or domain-specific reports. Recent work therefore develops active evaluators that seek missing evidence and update their grounds for judgment before deciding. We bring these advances together through Agent-as-a-Judge, focusing on how evaluators construct and control checking processes within the broader LLM-based judging landscape. We define the scope through evaluation-directed checks and the use of their results, covering both structured workflows and observation-driven control. We organize the design space by multi-agent collaboration, tool integration, memory, and planning, and show how these mechanisms supply the checks and evidence on which a verdict rests. We consolidate published scores and reproduce missing entries for key agentic judges; the comparison reveals uneven agentic gains and motivates dedicated agentic evaluation. We conclude by characterizing application demands and open challenges in cost, reliability, safety, and governance that condition trusted deployment of agentic judges at scale.
items.author: Runyang You, Hongru Cai, Caiqi Zhang, Qiancheng Xu, Meng Liu, Tiezheng Yu, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Li

items.title: FEND: Far-End Detection in Outbound Voice AI Calls
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.18050v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a conversational Voice AI agent places an outbound call, the far end may be a live person, a voicemail greeting, an interactive voice response (IVR) system, or increasingly another AI system answering on the callee's behalf. Standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) reports only whether a human or a machine picked up, a design meant for human call centres, where one machine is as uninteresting as another. That single bit does not tell a Voice AI agent what to do, since leaving a voicemail message, navigating an IVR and holding a short exchange with another AI are three different actions and a two-valued label cannot distinguish them. In 1,000 randomly sampled calls from our own outbound deployment, a live person answered 48.1%, a voicemail system 44.6%, an AI 6.9% and an IVR 0.4%. Our proposed framework, FEND, reads the far end's audio and its streaming transcript and runs one detector for each automated class (voicemail, IVR, AI callee), with human the default when nothing fires, returning a single label within 20 seconds. On a public benchmark the voicemail components reach 100% accuracy without ever misclassifying a live human, where Asterisk's AMD misclassifies 30 to 66% of them. For the AI callee, acoustic features do not transfer across recording conditions, but speech timing does, separating AI from human at 0.952 ROC-AUC, because synthesised speech leaves far shorter gaps between words. On production traffic, separating a live person from any automated far end reaches F1 0.979, and only 2.9% of live people are given an automated label, the error that matters most for an agent acting on the result.
items.author: Abhishek Kumar, Suraj Agrawal, Aashraya Sachdeva

items.title: Toward Universal Translatability: On the Statistical Ontology of Generative AI
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17963v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper argues that the problem of translation functions both as a point of origin and as a normative horizon for contemporary generative AI. In current discourse around ''world models,'' their attainment is framed as the achievement of internal consistency, cross-modal alignment, and physical grounding. Taken together, these demands converge on an ideal of the model as a universal translation machine capable of establishing lossless correspondences across linguistic, visual, and physical representation spaces. I show that this ideal presupposes a metaphysical commitment that I call a statistical ontology: the belief that reality has an underlying, computable statistical structure that can be recovered through sufficient data and modeling, rather than being shaped and accessed through situated human interpretation and labor. Tracing this commitment back to Warren Weaver's 1949 Memorandum on machine translation, I outline how translation was historically recast as code deciphering and, later, as the alignment of probability distributions across structured outputs. Finally, I contrast this paradigm with approaches in Translation Studies that foreground opacity, power asymmetries, and the translator's positionality. I argue that generative AI's statistical ontology is pre-Kantian, pre-critical and obscures the infrastructures and human labor that make machine translatability---as alignment---possible in the first place.
items.author: Katia Schwerzmann

items.title: In the Eye of the Beholder: Human Label Variation in Textual and Visual Entailment
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human Label Variation (HLV) is increasingly recognised as an informative signal that reflects meaningful differences in how people interpret the same input. While HLV has been studied extensively in Natural Language Inference (NLI), much less is known about HLV in Visual Entailment (VE; Xie et al., 2019), where the textual premise is replaced by an image, keeping the hypothesis and label space fixed. We introduce VariNLI-VE, a dataset for studying how HLV changes between paired NLI and VE instances. We re-annotate a subset of originally neutral SNLI (Bowman et al., 2015) instances and their visual counterparts, with the same annotators evaluating both the textual and visual versions. Each annotation includes a label, confidence score, and explanation, yielding 2,250 annotations. Labels and explanations are collected jointly, providing ecologically valid explanations. Because the image may reveal information not stated in the text, one might expect disagreement to decrease in VE. Instead, we find no clear overall reduction: disagreement decreases for some instances while it increases for others. Explanations reveal further variation, as annotators can retain the same label while changing their rationale. When evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on the paired data, we find lower accuracy, weaker alignment with human label distributions, and generally higher uncertainty in VE than in NLI.
items.author: Monica Riedler, Jasmin Orth, Raffaella Bernardi, Barbara Plank

items.title: BLiMP-RO: A Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for Romanian
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17836v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating grammatical knowledge in language models requires benchmarks that cover diverse linguistic phenomena and are validated against human judgments. We introduce BLiMP-RO, a Romanian minimal-pair benchmark covering 50 grammatical phenomena across ten domains. It comprises 493 linguist-constructed sentence pairs, evaluated by native speakers in five experiments, and 5,942 additional semi-automatically generated, human-validated pairs. We further investigate grammatical generalization under limited linguistic input by training GPT-2 and GPT-BERT models from scratch on Romanian BabyBabelLM data and a newly collected corpus of 10 million words from child-targeted video captions. Increasing caption training data yields approximately 9 percentage points of accuracy improvement per tenfold increase in corpus size. At matched data sizes, BabyBabelLM generally outperforms video captions, while GPT-BERT consistently outperforms GPT-2. Our findings highlight how training data quantity, composition, and model architecture shape grammatical generalization in Romanian.
items.author: Radu-Stefan Popa, Valentin Feroiu, Adina Camelia Bleotu, Sergiu Nisioi

items.title: PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17834v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI conference submissions grow rapidly, AI reviewers are being considered as an alternative. However, simply imitating human reviewing is problematic because reviewing serves multiple purposes, including evaluating papers' soundness, interestingness, and clarity, the last two of which are subjective. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating soundness, the most important and objective criterion, and define the learning objective as jointly maximizing (1) precision, based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points, and (2) recall, the coverage of high-quality reference review points. Under this problem formulation, we construct a quality-labeled review point dataset, PaperSound-23K, using 1K ICLR submissions and 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. Using this dataset, we train an AI reviewer model, PaperCritic, through reinforcement learning with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. Our experiments show that PaperCritic outperforms frontier models and models trained with other AI reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set. Surprisingly, learning to review ICLR submissions also transfers to reviewing Nature-family papers and even to out-of-domain reviewing tasks (e.g., code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing).
items.author: Hyun Ryu, Ji Yong Cho, Eunho Yang, Moontae Lee, June Yong Yang, Sean Welleck, Carolyn Rose

items.title: AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17811v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by reviewers to highlight weaknesses during the reviewing process, and their outputs often shape the reviews that humans submit. Prior work studies how LLM reviews align with human ones, yet we know little about which parts of a paper these models actually criticize. In this work, we investigate 2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR, and show that the latest GPT and Claude models draw about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix. This behavior holds across the API, coding-agent, and web access methods for using LLMs to review a paper. In contrast, we find that humans draw only 8.4% of their weaknesses from the appendix, and these weaknesses primarily revolve around a paper's presentation and content related to its core idea. Meanwhile, LLMs draw weaknesses from deep in the appendix that concern fine-grained technical details not central to the paper's contributions. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to the scholarly discourse on AI reviews. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/cincynlp/review_appendix.
items.author: Saptarshi Ghosh, Mohammad Saim, Tianyu Jiang

items.title: RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), query rewriting serves as a core interface that aligns user intent with external knowledge bases, and its effectiveness directly determines overall system performance. However, generative retrieval faces three critical challenges in real-world deployment: noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly optimizing discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding-control parameters, and the limited generalization of static rewriting strategies under semantically complex scenarios. To address these issues, we propose RAG-FGO, a dynamic optimization framework for generative retrieval strategies. RAG-FGO formulates query rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box optimization problem in a mixed discrete-continuous space, and represents prompt templates and decoding parameters as adaptively optimizable query-rewriting agents. The framework performs global search to enable semantic jumps and structural reorganization that escape local optima, while applying local perturbations for fine-grained alignment and precise refinement. In addition, RAG-FGO introduces an elite-preserving memory pool that accumulates high-quality strategies across iterations, thereby mitigating the impact of stochasticity and noisy feedback on optimization stability. Experimental results on a diverse suite of benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method, supporting its applicability to complex semantic retrieval tasks.
items.author: Qigan Sun, Xudong Wang, Chaoning Zhang, Chenghao Li, Jiaquan Zhang, Jiehui Xie, Sungyoung Lee, Jie Zou, Ning Xie, Peng Wang, Yang Yang, Heng Tao Shen

items.title: See Every Block Once: Variance-Reduced Post-Training for Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17754v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Policy gradient methods are widely used to align large language model outputs with human preferences, but the log-likelihoods they require cannot be directly computed in Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs). MDLM post-training therefore relies on a surrogate objective based on the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and recent work estimates a blockwise variant of this objective via Monte Carlo methods to support blockwise generation. However, existing estimation schemes randomly sample the block index, so they may evaluate the same block more than once and leave some blocks unevaluated. This introduces variance arising from block selection into the estimates. In this work, we propose a full-block estimator that evaluates every block exactly once and averages the results. We theoretically show that the proposed estimator remains unbiased while eliminating the between-group variance arising from block selection, thereby achieving lower variance than the baseline for the same sample size. In experiments on five benchmarks spanning mathematics, planning, and coding, our method achieves the highest accuracy on four benchmarks and outperforms the random block sampling baseline by an average of 12.79 points.
items.author: Yunzhen He, Hiroaki Yamagiwa, Hidetoshi Shimodaira

items.title: What Do Multilingual Self-Supervised Speech Encoders Know About Sentence Meaning?
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) have been scaled up to thousands of languages and millions of hours of audio, yet little is known about how these models structure semantic knowledge across languages. In this work, we probe sentence-level semantics in massively multilingual S3Ms across 76 languages, using linear maps from frozen speech representations into a frozen text embedding space, evaluated by cross-modal retrieval. Sentence meaning is linearly accessible but highly uneven across languages and resource tiers. Cross-lingual probes can match language-specific probes on languages never seen in probe training, but per-model monolingual decodability does not predict transfer. Within the OmniASR wav2vec family, scaling from 300M--7B disproportionately benefits high-resource languages, and ASR tuning sharply improves semantic decodability while making representations more language-specific. However, semantic content is entangled with acoustics, inflating apparent performance on single-speaker corpora.
items.author: Kevin Krahn, Eric Fosler-Lussier

items.title: Small Open-Weight Language Models for Crowd Decision-Making: Capabilities and Limits of Output-Level Fusion and Linguistic Aggregation
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17589v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small open-weight language models can run crowd decision-making (CDM) on an institution's own infrastructure, which keeps the checkpoint, the inference settings and the opinions under its control. Their judgements vary across repeated queries; whether repeating and aggregating them, often through the 2-tuple linguistic representation, settles the decision rather than the labels is untested. Five open-weight models of 8-36B total parameters on one consumer GPU and a hosted reference classify 474 TripAdvisor reviews of four London restaurants ten times each; three open-weight models repeat the protocol on 600 reviews of twelve Madrid restaurants. Continuous evaluations preserve resolution: snapping each review leaves 5 distinct values against 21-65, and snapping at every level at most two collective values. Sensitivity to the participants persists once run-to-run variability is reduced: in London, redrawing the reviewers keeps the winner on 47-81% of replicas against 86-100% for redrawing the runs. With simultaneous intervals over every pair of alternatives under crowd resampling, no system on either corpus names a single winner: in London every system keeps all four restaurants as candidates, and in Madrid the candidate sets hold five to eight of the twelve. Extra runs and output-level fusion stabilize the winner but do not remove that sensitivity, and the fusion does not beat its best member. The three larger open-weight models name the hosted reference's London winner and at least match its per-review correlation with the reviewers' stars, so small open-weight models can support local CDM, reported as candidate sets with margins rather than forced rankings.
items.author: David Herrera-Poyatos, Cristina Zuheros, Carlos Pel\'aez-Gonz\'alez, Andr\'es Herrera-Poyatos, Rosana Montes, Francisco Herrera

items.title: CamSpokenNLI: A Pilot Resource for Cross-Variety Transfer Evaluation in Cameroon Pidgin English and Camfranglais
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17573v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cameroon Pidgin English (a West African Pidgin English variety) and Camfranglais are widely used in Cameroon, yet to our knowledge, neither has a dedicated spoken Natural Language Inference (NLI) resource. We introduce CamSpokenNLI, a pilot dataset of 114 scenario-matched spoken NLI items in each variety (228 in total), recorded by one native speaker from Buea. Each item pairs premise audio and text with a hypothesis, an NLI label, and English glosses. The author assigned labels, so the dataset is an exploratory resource rather than a mature benchmark. The NLI experiments use the reference text; the audio is evaluated separately. XLM-RoBERTa baselines with five-fold item-level cross-validation reach 44.7% on Pidgin and 46.2% on Camfranglais (chance 33.3%). Still, neither is statistically distinguishable from hypothesis-only input, so hypothesis wording may account for much of the accuracy. Under disjoint-item cross-variety transfer, where a test item's counterpart is never seen in training, accuracy is 40.1% (Pidgin to Camfranglais) and 45.6% (Camfranglais to Pidgin). A counterpart-leak audit raises this to 60-64%, illustrating how counterpart leakage can overstate transfer. Zero-shot Whisper transcription of the recordings performs poorly: the best word error rates are 66.6% for Pidgin and 45.5% for Camfranglais, and with automatic language identification, Whisper Large-v3 labels 93 of 114 Pidgin recordings as Yoruba or Swahili. Together, the results suggest that such resources need disjoint-item evaluation and hypothesis-only controls, and that speech recognition must be adapted to these varieties before spoken NLI can be tested end to end.
items.author: Tiani Pekins Ebika

items.title: Poetry 'resurrection' from LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17464v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In an era where linguistic creativity is challenged by algorithmic authorship, we pose a provocative question: can artificial intelligence (AI) write an infinite poem? We set up two experiments to investigate the quantitative and qualitative output produced by AI utilizing couplets that evidence a poetic relationship between end words, the only variation in a strict anaphoric, litany structure. Our results show that while AI can generate interesting pairings, it still falls short of human-level creativity and understanding of poetic relationships. We offer commentary and a brief survey of the field of computational poetry experiments, tracing back authorial intention and distinctions of 'natural' and 'artificial' poetry, as well as justifying why couplet form is suited to testing AI's poetic output. Experiment 1 relies on manual prompting and co-creation to extend the original poem, which is developed into an animated webpage installation and interactive artwork. Experiment 2 reliably achieves automated output reaching the 1000 benchmark via an alternative method of using an LLM in combination with semantic similarity, of which Method 2 demonstrates a higher capacity for semantic and quantitative poetic output. These experiments highlight the limitations of current LLMs' generation capacity at the word level but also suggest that poetry will also respond and revive by incorporating AI workflows.
items.author: Vincent Cellucci, Peter van der Putten

items.title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.17461v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.
items.author: Yang Wang, Xiao Wang, Yiqi Liu, Chenghao Xiao, Eleni Vasilaki, Goran Nenadic, Chenghua Lin

items.title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.19095v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Chatbot Arena gives each language model one Bradley-Terry score, which fixes how often any model should beat any other. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are compared on the few details in which they differ, so votes between them are more decisive than their scores imply, exactly for the comparison a lab cares about, a new version against the old one. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later points the same way, and the effect survives tie, prompt, topic and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. Plain scores leave the odds between relatives about 9% too close to even on held-out votes; a correction with four to six parameters roughly halves this and predicts held-out votes better, mostly by modeling ties, while the leaderboard order barely moves; frozen and carried to new releases, its gains in head-to-head odds are too small for our test to establish. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16), less so within a prompt.
items.author: Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose, Aishwarya Bose, Sandip Nandi

items.title: High-Dimensional Online Calibration from Harmonic Weights
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.07740v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the online calibration of multidimensional forecasts over an arbitrary convex set $Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ relative to an arbitrary error norm $\|\cdot\|_L$. For forecasting $d$ binary outcomes simultaneously ($Y=[0,1]^d$), we give the first algorithm that achieves $\varepsilon$-calibration in a number of rounds that is polynomial in $d$ for every fixed accuracy. It requires $d^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ rounds, exponentially improving the dimension dependence of previous bounds. For multi-class forecasting ($Y=\Delta_d$), we obtain the same $d^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ rate, improving the $d^{\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^2)}$ bounds of Peng and Fishelson, Golowich, Mohri, and Schneider.
  Our algorithm is simple: on each round, it outputs a harmonically weighted distribution over harmonically smoothed past outcomes. The same algorithm works for every forecast set and error norm. More generally, it achieves $\varepsilon$-calibration after $\exp(O(\gamma(Y,L)/\varepsilon))$ rounds, where $\gamma(Y,L)$ is a geometric parameter defined by a matrix discrepancy problem. The harmonic weights are motivated by the fact that the discrete Hilbert transform matrix achieves the optimal discrepancy up to a universal constant, simultaneously for every $L$. This optimality result may be of independent interest.
  The same harmonic responses also yield an algorithm for high-dimensional Blackwell approachability. Its guarantees are governed by a sharpened geometric parameter that captures the joint geometry of the outcome and action sets.
items.author: Maxwell Fishelson, Mehryar Mohri

items.title: The Alignment Illusion in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.30210v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Layer-wise visual-text similarity in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is widely interpreted as evidence that the language model progressively integrates visual content into a shared representation space. This reading rests on the assumption that scalar alignment scores reflect content-level cross-modal interaction. To test this assumption, we apply controlled interventions to the visual stream. Across 13 MLLMs from five families spanning 0.5B to 72B parameters, replacing projector-output visual tokens with Gaussian noise sharply reduces task accuracy, yet four standard scalar measures (CKA, SVCCA, MIR, and the leading principal-angle cosine) fail to consistently separate the corrupted stream from the original. We call this failure the alignment illusion and trace it to the shared language-model pathway: anisotropic MLP down-projections pull visual and text tokens toward common output directions, producing weight-induced alignment. We introduce the principal-angle gap (PA gap), defined as the difference between the top two principal-angle cosines, to distinguish leading-direction dominance from the broader overlap observed with structured visual content. Under graded visual corruption, the PA gap tracks task accuracy more consistently than the scalar scores we consider; under a structured but irrelevant image, it further exposes regimes in which internal geometry and task accuracy come apart. Internal visual-text alignment in MLLMs is therefore best read as a geometric diagnostic of the visual stream inside the language model rather than a direct proxy for content-level cross-modal interaction, and is most informative when calibrated by controlled task evidence.
items.author: Hong-Han Wang, Yuntao Wang, Hu Ding

items.title: UltraBench 2: Towards Robust Evaluation of Vision Foundation Models on Ultrasound
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.28610v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Benchmarking is an increasingly critical part of research in machine learning and the domains where it is applied, including healthcare. Yet, despite the steady development of new ultrasound foundation models in recent years, the development of well-designed benchmarks to evaluate them has lagged behind. This deficiency has led to fragmented and inconsistent evaluations of competing models, making it difficult to measure progress. To address this issue, we introduce UltraBench 2, a comprehensive benchmark with wide anatomical and task coverage, and a focus on standardization, reproducibility, and ease-of-use. Using this benchmark, we compare existing vision foundation models for ultrasound image analysis. Our analyses demonstrate that ultrasound-specific pretraining still leads on classification, but that state-of-the-art general-purpose models have drawn level on segmentation.
items.author: Ashwath Radhachandran, Adam Tupper, Christian Gagn\'e, William Speier

items.title: Local Spike Timing Enables Gradient-based Learning in Neural Microcircuits
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.08070v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The brain uses discrete spikes for dynamic computation, yet in the fields of computational neuroscience and brain-inspired computing, how neural microcircuits (NMCs) solve temporal credit assignment using local spike timing remains a fundamental open question. Dominant spiking neural network (SNN) approaches circumvent this by approximating backpropagation through surrogate gradients, decoupling learning from biological spike timing. In order to integrate seemingly incompatible spike timing and continuous gradients, we reformulate temporal credit assignment as a state separation problem: extracting task-required components induced by historical perturbations directly from the current neural state. This enables an online feedback learning framework for NMCs through a gradient tunneling (GT) algorithm and the lead-lag expansion technique that derives credit assignment from local synaptic spike timing, while remaining compatible with ANN-SNN hybrid architectures. Experimentally, GT-trained NMCs excel at long-timescale evidence integration and noise-robust memory retention, and perform comparably to leading SNN online learning methods on real-world benchmarks with far fewer parameters. The proposed framework addresses the two-decade-old NMC feedback learning problem and suggests a computational theory for the brain's temporal credit assignment mechanisms.
items.author: Xiangnan Zhang, Jingxin Liu, Ranqi Lu, Jingyu Liu, Qunxi Dong, Fuze Tian, Lixian Zhu, Bin Hu, Bj\"orn W. Schuller

items.title: BBOWP-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Black-Box Optimization Word Problems
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.02612v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Formulating an optimization problem strongly affects final solution quality, yet good formulations usually require substantial expertise. Recent studies have explored automatically deriving optimization problems from natural-language descriptions, but existing benchmarks focus on settings where objectives and constraints can be written explicitly as mathematical expressions. Many practically important problems are naturally treated as black-box optimization (BBO) problems, in which only objective values are observable, and the functional form is unavailable. In BBO, search space design (as part of problem formulation) and optimization algorithm selection are crucial for problem-solving. Automating these processes with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. We introduce Black-Box Optimization Word Problems (BBOWP), a novel problem setting in which a system must infer both a search space and an optimization algorithm from a natural-language description of a black-box optimization task. To support research on this setting, we establish the BBOWP Benchmark Suite (BBOWP-Bench), a dataset and evaluation framework for BBOWP. Each instance combines a natural-language problem description, an executable evaluation environment, and a human-designed reference formulation, allowing evaluation of both search-space design and algorithm selection. Using this benchmark, we evaluate LLMs on the joint formulation of search spaces and optimizers from natural-language descriptions across multiple BBO domains. We show that current LLMs vary their optimizer choice with the evaluation budget, though they sometimes struggle with search space design, particularly in identifying important variables and balancing their ranges when the problem description is less informative or the search space is highly problem-specific. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/shiralab/bbowp-bench.
items.author: Yutaro Yamada, Kei Hiroshima, Nozomu Yoshinari, Kento Uchida, Shinichi Shirakawa

items.title: MMAO-Cls: Metabolic Multi-Agent Optimization for Joint Feature Selection and Classifier Tuning
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.01539v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This paper studies whether the Metabolic Multi-Agent Optimizer (MMAO) can act as a credible outer-loop optimizer for classification model selection. We propose MMAO-Cls, a mixed-space realization in which each agent jointly encodes a binary feature mask and classifier hyperparameters, while private energy, communal budget, role drift, and lifecycle turnover are mapped to the accuracy-complexity tradeoff of wrapper learning. The implementation is strengthened by deriving feature-budget adaptation from feature-information priors and by regularizing validation reward with both subset compactness and train-validation overfitting gap. We evaluate MMAO-Cls on seven standard tabular benchmarks with three seeds each and compare it against RandomSearch, GA-lite, PSO-lite, and an endogenous no-sharing ablation. On the aggregate validation objective, MMAO-Cls ranks second ($0.9433$) behind GA-lite ($0.9446$). On held-out test performance, it reaches mean score $0.8882$, improving over RandomSearch ($0.8808$) and GA-lite ($0.8857$), remaining close to PSO-lite ($0.8874$) and the no-sharing ablation ($0.8900$), while using the most compact mean held-out feature subset among all compared methods (feature ratio $0.4881$). Pairwise tests show that these margins are not yet statistically significant. The results support MMAO's applicability to classification and compact mixed-space search, while the contribution of communal sharing to held-out performance remains unresolved.
items.author: Jinliang Xu, Liping Ma

items.title: Kernel-based potential mean-field games with unbiased random Fourier $U$-statistics
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.29371v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the subclass of potential mean-field games in which the running interaction cost and the terminal target cost are both expressed through reproducing-kernel maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) penalties, and develop a computational framework that exploits this kernel structure. Both costs are estimated from finite-sample empirical distributions using a random Fourier U-statistic representation that is unbiased and has linear cost in the batch size. The drift of the controlled diffusion is parametrized by a neural network and trained via stochastic gradient descent. For population near-minimizers we prove convergence to the terminal-constrained problem as the penalty diverges, and show that the same limit is recovered almost surely when such controls are evaluated on independent finite samples under explicit coupling conditions on the penalty, random-feature count and sample size. The framework includes the kernel-MMD-penalty Schr{\"o}dinger bridge problem as the special case of a vanishing interaction cost. Numerical experiments illustrate the method on the Schr{\"o}dinger bridge problem in dimensions up to one hundred, and on an electric vehicle charging coordination problem with per-vehicle physical heterogeneity, where a control-dependent aggregate-demand cost produces a trade-off between peak normalized charging power and the terminal service level.
items.author: Yumiharu Nakano

items.title: SA-RAG: Structuring Noisy Conversations for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.24366v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely adopted in conversational applications. However, their reliance on parametric knowledge limits reliability in real-world scenarios that require dynamic or domain-specific information. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this limitation by incorporating external knowledge during generation, but existing RAG methods often struggle with noisy or irrelevant contexts, as they typically assume that high-quality structures are already available. In this work, we propose Structure-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation (SA-RAG), a principled structure induction and generation framework that constructs reliable intermediate structures directly from noisy conversational data. SA-RAG uses tables as compact and controllable structured representations. We introduce a quality-aware structure induction framework that jointly models semantic and structural consistency. Furthermore, we explore both training-free and training-based structure generation strategies to further improve structure quality while maintaining fidelity. Experiments on two noisy real-world datasets show that SA-RAG significantly outperforms existing RAG baselines. Further analysis highlights that high-quality structural representations are crucial for robust RAG applications.
items.author: Kaiqiao Han, LuAn Tang, Renliang Sun, Peng Yuan, Wei Cheng, Haoyu Wang, Wei Wang, Yizhou Sun, Haifeng Chen

items.title: mlr3torch: A Deep Learning Framework in R based on mlr3 and torch
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.18152v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Deep learning (DL) has become a cornerstone of modern machine learning (ML) praxis. We introduce the R package mlr3torch, which is an extensible DL framework for the mlr3 ecosystem. It is built upon the torch package, and simplifies the definition, training, and evaluation of neural networks for both tabular data and generic tensors (e.g., images) for classification and regression. The package implements predefined architectures, and torch models can easily be converted to mlr3 learners. It also allows users to define neural networks as graphs. This representation is based on the graph language defined in mlr3pipelines and allows users to define the entire modeling workflow, including preprocessing, data augmentation, and network architecture, in a single graph. Through its integration into the mlr3 ecosystem, the package allows for convenient resampling, benchmarking, preprocessing, and more. We explain the package's design and features and show how to customize and extend it to new problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the package's capabilities using three use cases, namely hyperparameter tuning, fine-tuning, and defining architectures for multimodal data. Finally, we present some runtime benchmarks.
items.author: Sebastian Fischer, Lukas Burk, Carson Zhang, Bernd Bischl, Martin Binder

items.title: DRTriton: Large-Scale Synthetic Data Driven Reinforcement Learning for Triton Kernel Generation
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.21465v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Developing efficient CUDA kernels is a fundamental yet challenging task in the generative AI industry. Recent research leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically convert PyTorch reference implementations to CUDA kernels, significantly reducing engineering effort. State-of-the-art LLMs, such as GPT-5.2 and Claude-Sonnet-4.5, still struggle with this task. To address this challenge, we propose DRTriton, a scalable learning framework for training LLMs to convert PyTorch programs into highly optimized Triton kernels, which are then compiled to CUDA kernels at runtime. DRTriton consists of three key components: (i) a data synthetic algorithm CSP-DAG that guarantees full coverage and unbiased uniform sampling over the operator space with controlled difficulty; (ii) a curriculum RL framework with decoupled rewards that jointly optimizes conversion success rate and execution speed; and (iii) a test-time search algorithm that further improves the execution speed of the generated Triton kernels. With a warmup stage of SFT on limited PyTorch-Triton pairs curated using existing LLMs, DRTriton trained by RL on synthesized PyTorch programs generalizes effectively to real-world CUDA kernels that are challenging even for human experts. Experimental results show that DRTriton-7B achieves speedup over PyTorch on 92% of KernelBench Level 2 tasks, compared to 23% for GPT-5.2 and 19% for Claude-Sonnet-4.5.
items.author: Siqi Guo, Ming Lin, Tianbao Yang

items.title: Auto-differentiable data assimilation: Co-learning of states, dynamics, and filtering algorithms
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.20891v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Data assimilation algorithms estimate the state of a dynamical system from partial observations, where the successful performance of these algorithms hinges on costly parameter tuning and on employing an accurate model for the dynamics. This paper introduces a framework for jointly learning the state, dynamics, and parameters of filtering algorithms in data assimilation through a process we refer to as auto-differentiable filtering. The framework leverages a theoretically motivated loss function that enables learning from partial, noisy observations via gradient-based optimization using auto-differentiation. We further demonstrate how several well-known data assimilation methods can be learned or tuned within this framework. To underscore the versatility of auto-differentiable filtering, we perform experiments on dynamical systems spanning multiple scientific domains, such as the Clohessy-Wiltshire equations from aerospace engineering, the Lorenz-96 system from atmospheric science, the generalized Lotka-Volterra equations from systems biology, and the two-layer quasi-geostrophic model from geophysical fluid dynamics. Finally, we provide guidelines for practitioners to customize our framework according to their observation model, accuracy requirements, and computational budget.
items.author: Melissa Adrian, Daniel Sanz-Alonso, Rebecca Willett

items.title: On sparsity, extremal structure, and monotonicity properties of Wasserstein and Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport plans
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.16265v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This note gives a self-contained overview of some key properties of the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance, compared with the standard linear optimal transport (OT) framework. More specifically, I explore the following questions: are GW optimal transport plans sparse? under what conditions does there exist an optimal plan supported on a permutation? do optimal plans satisfy a form of cyclical monotonicity? In particular, I present the conditionally negative/positive definite (CND/CPD) properties and show that, when they hold, there exist GW optimal plans that are sparse and supported on a permutation. In the last section, I also give examples where no permutation is optimal when the CND or CPD assumption is dropped.
items.author: Titouan Vayer (COMPACT)

items.title: Adaptive Power Iteration Method for Differentially Private PCA
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.11454v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study $\left(\epsilon,\delta\right)$-differentially private algorithms for the problem of approximately computing the top singular vector of a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ where each row of $A$ is a data point in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Following Dwork-Talwar-Thakurta-Zhang (STOC 2014), we consider the privacy model where neighboring inputs differ by one single row. We give a novel algorithm that achieves beyond-worst-case guarantees for input matrices with low coherence, which is a structural property of matrices in many applications, including but not limited to i.i.d. data. Our algorithm contributes to the extensive literature on private power iteration methods, where we introduce a new filtering technique which adapts to this coherence parameter. Our work departs from and complements the work by Hardt-Roth (STOC 2013) which achieves beyond-worst-case guarantees for the more restrictive privacy model where neighboring inputs differ in one single entry by at most 1.
items.author: Ta Duy Nguyen, Alina Ene, Huy Le Nguyen

items.title: HetCCL: Efficient LLM Training on Heterogeneous Vendor GPUs
items.summary:
arXiv:2601.22585v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The rapid growth of large language models is driving organizations to expand their GPU clusters, often with GPUs from multiple vendors. However, current deep learning frameworks lack support for collective communication across heterogeneous GPUs, leading to inefficiency and higher costs. We present HetCCL, a collective communication library that unifies vendor-specific backends and enables RDMA-based communication across GPUs without requiring driver modifications. HetCCL introduces two novel mechanisms that enable cross-vendor communication while leveraging optimized vendor libraries, NVIDIA NCCL and AMD RCCL. Evaluations on a multi-vendor GPU cluster show that HetCCL matches NCCL and RCCL performance in homogeneous setups while uniquely scaling in heterogeneous environments, enabling practical, high-performance training with both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs without changes to existing deep learning applications.
items.author: Heehoon Kim, Chris Jaehwan Lee, Taejeoung Kim, Jongwon Park, Jinpyo Kim, Pyongwon Suh, Ryan H. Choi, Sangwoo Lee, Jaejin Lee

items.title: Toric geometry of ReLU neural networks
items.summary:
arXiv:2509.05894v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Given a continuous piecewise linear function $f:\mathbb{R}^{n_0} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a fixed architecture of feedforward ReLU neural networks, the exact function realization problem asks when a network of that architecture realizes $f$. In contrast, expressivity concerns characterizing all functions exactly realizable by a given architecture. To address these questions systematically, we establish a connection between toric geometry and ReLU neural networks, allowing tools from algebraic geometry to analyze the structures. Starting with an unbiased ReLU network with rational weights, we define the ReLU fan, the ReLU toric variety, and the ReLU Cartier divisor associated with the network. This work also relates the tropical and the toric geometry: the former captures combinatorial data of ReLU networks, while the latter recovers the underlying geometric structure. As an application, we obtain a complete characterization of the functions realizable by unbiased shallow ReLU networks with rational weights. The characterization is expressed in terms of intersection numbers of ReLU Cartier divisors with torus-invariant curves and leads to a decomposition of piecewise-linear functions into shallow and non-shallow components.
items.author: Yaoying Fu

items.title: Training Language Model Agents to Find Vulnerabilities with CTF-Dojo
items.summary:
arXiv:2508.18370v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities when trained within executable runtime environments, notably excelling at software engineering tasks through verified feedback loops. Yet, scalable and generalizable execution-grounded environments remain scarce, limiting progress in training more capable ML agents. We introduce CTF-Dojo, the first large-scale executable runtime tailored for training LLMs with verifiable feedback, featuring 658 fully functional Capture-The-Flag (CTF)-style challenges containerized in Docker with guaranteed reproducibility. To enable rapid scaling without manual intervention, we develop CTF-Forge, an automated pipeline that transforms publicly available artifacts into ready-to-use execution environments in minutes, eliminating weeks of expert configuration traditionally required. We trained LLM-based agents on just 486 high-quality, execution-verified trajectories from CTF-Dojo, achieving up to 9.9% absolute gains over strong baselines across three competitive benchmarks: InterCode-CTF, NYU CTF Bench, and Cybench. Our best-performing 32B model reaches 31.9% Pass@1, establishing a new open-weight state-of-the-art that rivals frontier models like DeepSeek-V3-0324 and Gemini-2.5-Flash. By framing CTF-style tasks as a benchmark for executable-agent learning, CTF-Dojo demonstrates that execution-grounded training signals are not only effective but pivotal in advancing high-performance ML agents without dependence on costly proprietary systems.
items.author: Terry Yue Zhuo, Dingmin Wang, Hantian Ding, Varun Kumar, Zijian Wang

items.title: Cyber-Zero: Training Cybersecurity Agents without Runtime
items.summary:
arXiv:2508.00910v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in software engineering tasks when trained with executable runtime environments, particularly in resolving GitHub issues. However, such runtime environments are often unavailable in other domains, especially cybersecurity, where challenge configurations and execution contexts are ephemeral or restricted. We present Cyber-Zero, the first runtime-free framework for synthesizing high-quality agent trajectories to train cybersecurity LLMs. Cyber-Zero leverages publicly available CTF writeups and employs persona-driven LLM simulation to reverse-engineer runtime behaviors and generate realistic, long-horizon interaction sequences without actual environments. Using trajectories synthesized by Cyber-Zero, we train LLM-based agents that achieve up to 11.4% absolute performance gains over baseline models on three prominent CTF benchmarks: InterCode-CTF, NYU CTF Bench, and Cybench. Our best model, Cyber-Zero-32B, establishes new state-of-the-art performance among open-weight models, matching the capabilities of proprietary systems like DeepSeek-V3-0324 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet while offering superior cost-effectiveness, and demonstrating that runtime-free trajectory synthesis can effectively democratize the development of state-of-the-art cybersecurity agents.
items.author: Terry Yue Zhuo, Dingmin Wang, Hantian Ding, Varun Kumar, Zijian Wang

items.title: Recovering the Euclidean Geometry of High-Dimensional Data Under Heterogeneous Noise
items.summary:
arXiv:2507.18520v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Pairwise Euclidean distances provide a simple geometric representation of high-dimensional data and underlie many data analysis methods, including clustering, visualization, and manifold learning. However, in real-world applications, these distances can be severely corrupted by heterogeneous noise, where different data points are subject to different, and potentially large, noise levels. Such noise distorts the distances inhomogeneously, leading to a misrepresentation of the underlying data geometry. In this work, we ask whether the underlying clean Euclidean geometry can nevertheless be recovered from the corrupted pairwise distances. We answer this question affirmatively, showing that, perhaps surprisingly, such recovery is possible across a broad class of high-dimensional settings with underlying low-dimensional geometry, even when the noise magnitudes vary substantially across observations. We develop a principled approach for recovering the clean pairwise distances, without prior knowledge of either the clean data structure or the noise distribution, and establish probabilistic recovery guarantees. In particular, the recovery error converges to zero at polynomial rates as the feature dimension and dataset size increase simultaneously. Experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate accurate recovery of the Euclidean geometry in challenging regimes and improved robustness of downstream methods that rely on pairwise distances. When applied to real single-cell RNA sequencing data, our method reliably recovers local neighborhood structure, enabling accurate nearest-neighbor identification used in many downstream analyses.
items.author: Keyi Li, Yuval Kluger, Boris Landa

items.title: Bias-Optimal Bounds for Stochastic Gradient Descent
items.summary:
arXiv:2505.17965v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The non-asymptotic analysis of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) typically yields bounds that decompose into a bias term and a variance term. In this work, we focus on the bias component and study the extent to which SGD can match the optimal convergence behavior of deterministic gradient descent. Assuming only (strong) convexity and smoothness of the objective, we derive new bounds for the full range of constant step-sizes $\gamma L \in (0,2)$. This includes critical and large step-size regimes that were previously unexplored without additional variance assumptions, in both the convex and strongly convex cases. Those bounds are bias-optimal, in the sense that the bias term coincides with the worst-case rate of gradient descent, for all non-critical step-sizes. For critical step-sizes, we show that no bounds can be obtained with an optimal bias term, but that this optimal bias can be approximated arbitrarily closely. As an immediate application, we provide new complexity bounds for the Stochastic Proximal algorithm, without the need of regularity assumptions.
items.author: Daniel Cortild, Lucas Ketels, Juan Peypouquet, Guillaume Garrigos

items.title: FedSharp: Byzantine Robust Decentralized Federated Learning Under Noisy Channel
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.05546v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) eliminates the central aggregation server but remains vulnerable to non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, Byzantine attacks, and channel noise. We show that channel noise accumulates as models propagate across nodes and becomes increasingly significant as the learning rate decays. Moreover, accumulated noise enables Byzantine attackers to exploit loss-based model selection by mimicking the average of the honest models. To address these challenges, we propose FedSharp (screened, hop-aware, averaged, ranked, proximal), a robust DFL framework. In FedSharp, each node keeps the latest models received from its 2b predecessors, which guarantees at least b honest candidates when at most b nodes are Byzantine. FedSharp screens suspicious models using their deviations from the coordinate-wise median, averages the b lowest-loss candidates to reduce the fresh channel-noise variance by a factor of b, and applies hop-aware gradient-norm regularization and proximal training to mitigate accumulated noise and non-IID drift. Experiments on a 100-node ring with 33 Byzantine nodes show that FedSharp achieves 93.5 to 94.9 percent accuracy on MNIST, compared with 29.4 to 38.1 percent for a state-of-the-art single-model-selection benchmark, and 32.8 to 48.8 percent on CIFAR-10, compared with 10.0 to 30.5 percent, across Gaussian and hidden attacks under IID and non-IID data. On MNIST, FedSharp comes within 1.3 percentage points of the benchmark operating without channel noise, and exceeds it under the hidden attack.
items.author: Ojaswi Sinha, Amin Farajzadeh, Animesh Yadav, Melike Erol-Kantarci

items.title: PATTERN Can Be Solved from Memory: Testing Graph Neural Networks on Unseen Patterns
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.15020v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: PATTERN asks graph neural networks to find a planted subgraph in a new host graph. The hosts change, but the benchmark draws just 100 patterns and reuses them across training and test splits. A lookup that extracts these patterns from the training labels achieves 96.6% class-weighted accuracy on the official test split, above every published result, without fitting a model or consulting the generator. On unseen patterns, the same lookup scores 50.6%. A matcher that also uses the generator reaches 99.2% on the official split. Among five graph networks we retrained, GRASS and PPGT go from the top two on the official split to the bottom two on unseen patterns. Each loses 8.1 percentage points even when familiar and unseen patterns are matched in size. Logistic regression on two-hop node statistics scores above every run of the five networks on unseen patterns. For CKGConv, the advantage follows the training patterns: it reappears with each of three independently drawn pattern libraries and disappears when every training and validation graph gets a new pattern. Generator-based inference also scores 82.3% on CLUSTER, compared with a published best of 81.6%. On Minesweeper's released board, four of eight planned chains produced samples within the time budget; none converged, but their pooled predictions reached 99.86% ROC AUC, above the published best of 99.55%. PATTERN's official split tests its intended task of finding familiar patterns in new graphs. We recommend reporting the same checkpoint's score on unseen patterns alongside it.
items.author: Amin Najafgholizadeh, Mohsen Afsharchi

items.title: Similar Predictive Fit but Different Latent Dynamics: Characterizing Learned Dynamical Structure in Personalized Models of Brain Disorders
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.10850v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As AI models move toward clinical decision-making and personalized treatment, understanding \emph{what} a model learns is important beyond predictive accuracy alone. We investigate whether personalized latent dynamics reveal clinically associated differences even when predictive fit is similar. A lightweight CNN--Transformer EEG foundation model pretrained on the Temple University EEG Corpus (TUEG) extracts segment-level representations. Using the Temple University Epilepsy Corpus (TUEP), representations are mapped to a shared latent-state space, and sparse multinomial logistic transition distributions (mLTD) are fit independently to each subject to obtain personalized transition-dependency graphs $W_n$. Analyses include $n{=}198$ subjects (99 epilepsy / 99 non-epilepsy). At $k{=}4$, epilepsy subjects exhibit substantially denser learned dependency structure ($p{=}1.1\times10^{-7}$), with the same pattern at $k{=}6$ (19.90 vs. 13.46; $p{=}5.2\times10^{-5}$). Graph-derived features provide moderate group discrimination under 5-fold subject-wise cross-validation (AUROC 0.68 at $k{=}4$; 0.65 at $k{=}6$). In contrast, held-out log-likelihood is nearly identical between groups at $k{=}4$ ($-0.992$ vs. $-0.991$; $p{=}0.95$), with similarly matched next-state prediction (AUROC 0.855 vs. 0.861; $p{=}0.54$). Thus, similar predictive fit does not imply similar learned dynamics: groups can be comparably predictable while differing substantially in the internal dynamical structure learned by personalized models. This distinction motivates evaluating learned structure alongside predictive performance in personalized clinical models.
items.author: Rita Huan-Ting Peng, Nhat Bui

items.title: Lightweight Semantic EEG Foundation Model for Frozen Cross-Disorder Transfer
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.05503v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large-scale EEG foundation models have demonstrated promising transferability across neurological disorders, but often require millions of parameters and substantial computational resources. In this paper, we present the Universal Semantic EEG Foundation Model (USE-FM), a lightweight EEG foundation model that learns transferable neural representations through self-supervised signal reconstruction on the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus (TUEG). After pretraining, the encoder is frozen and evaluated on two clinically distinct downstream tasks, abnormal EEG detection (TUAB) and epileptic seizure recognition (TUEP), using a unified frozen-transfer protocol against recent EEG foundation models, including LUNA-Base and CBraMod. With only 1.46 million parameters, approximately one-fifth the size of existing models, USE-FM achieves competitive overall performance, including strong sensitivity and F1-score on TUEP (SEN $75.00 \pm 14.14$, F1 $70.37 \pm 4.01$), while maintaining competitive performance on TUAB (AUC $85.24 \pm 5.61$). Beyond downstream classification, latent representation analysis using $k$-means clustering together with PCA and t-SNE demonstrates that USE-FM learns organized semantic EEG representations comparable to substantially larger foundation models. These results suggest that large-scale self-supervised pretraining enables lightweight architectures to learn transferable semantic EEG representations, providing a computationally efficient foundation for cross-disorder analysis and future clinical decision support in neurological disorders.
items.author: Rita Huan-Ting Peng, Nhat Bui

items.title: When a Flatness Proxy Is Not a Function: Robustness Certificates and Training Interventions
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.38540v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A valid curvature upper bound need not justify either a robustness certificate or an intervention on an intrinsic predictor property. We demonstrate this distinction for a last-layer relative-flatness proxy used in both settings. First, empirical-risk stationarity does not eliminate pointwise first-order loss terms: at a finite global empirical-risk minimum, the retained certificate expression underestimates a loss increase by over $210\times$. We derive a globally valid, gauge-invariant feature-space repair. Second, common-row softmax shifts preserve predictions and the exact contraction while making the proxy unbounded. Even standard reference-class choices double it on average relative to the centered representation. For a single fixed-feature example with at least three classes, scalar retuning generically cannot align the induced probability updates. Row centering gives the orbit-minimized bound and restores value and full-model gradient invariance under this symmetry. Across 45 paired one-step tests on algorithmic and image models, amplified shifts separate raw-regularized predictors while quotient-regularized predictors remain aligned. Long-horizon CIFAR-10 experiments show substantial, reversible suppression of generalization, while evidence for selective delay after memorization is less consistent. Together, these results show that validity as a curvature upper bound does not by itself justify either inversion into a robustness certificate or differentiation into an intrinsic training intervention.
items.author: Vicente Opazo

items.title: ReCo: When to Relocate Sensor Kits under Deployment Constraints -- A NILM Case Study
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.35075v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many sensing tasks obtain training labels only by deploying instruments in the field. With a limited number of sensor kits, a collection deadline, and measurement downtime at every move, the collector must repeatedly decide whether to stay at the current site or relocate. We study this decision in non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM), which estimates the power drawn by individual appliances from a home's main meter and is trained on data from homes temporarily fitted with appliance-level sub-meters. In NILM, appliance usage varies with the appliance, season and climate, and the value of new data depends on how diverse the combinations of target operation and background load are. To address this, we propose a constraint-based relocation framework and instantiate it for NILM as ReCo (Relocation by Coverage gain). ReCo counts new operating regimes in a joint target--background feature space, forecasts each home's future gain from the data collected so far, and each night weighs the gain of staying against the gain of moving elsewhere after the downtime. In replayed deployments on the Plegma dataset under two kit counts and two downtime costs, ReCo outperforms fixed-dwell and count-based schedules and a threshold rule using the same metric in every setting. Its advantage is not explained by collecting more days alone and is consistent with allocating the days to more valuable homes and periods.
items.author: Haokun Chen, Yu Tong, Yehai Chen

items.title: Attributing Cohen's d: Training Data Attribution for Disease-Related Effects in Normative Age Biomarkers
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.07729v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Normative age models are trained to predict chronological age in a nominally healthy cohort. In patients, the gap between predicted and chronological age is read as disease risk. We attribute the disease-related effect size of the age gap directly to individual training samples, rather than using a prediction-level loss as the attribution target. For the Cohen's d effect size, the resulting closed-form influence functional, validated against leave-one-out retraining, ranks training samples by their effect on held-out case-control separation.
